q: What is the IUPAC name of the ester shown?
h: An ester is named alkyl alkanoate: the group on the single-bonded O comes first, then the acyl part (which includes the C=O carbon) with -oate.
w: Split the ester at the single-bonded oxygen. The O-alkyl group is CH(CH3)2, isopropyl. The acyl part is CH3CH2C(=O)–, three carbons counting the carbonyl carbon, so it is propanoate: isopropyl propanoate.
x: This swaps the two halves: here the branched group is on the oxygen, not on the acyl side, and the O-alkyl group is not a straight propyl.
The acyl part has three carbons including the C=O carbon, not four; counting the oxygen-bearing CH as part of the acid chain gives the wrong parent.
1-Methylethyl is a correct name for isopropyl, but the acid part has three carbons (propanoate), not two (ethanoate); the C=O carbon must be counted.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the amide shown?
h: The parent chain is the acyl chain that includes the C=O carbon (C1). Groups on nitrogen get the locant N.
w: The acyl chain is C(=O)–CH2–CH(CH3)–CH3: four carbons with C1 = C=O, so butanamide with a methyl on C3. Nitrogen carries one ethyl and one methyl, each labeled N. Alphabetizing (ethyl before methyl) and combining the two methyls gives N-ethyl-N,3-dimethylbutanamide.
x: Numbering of an amide always starts at the carbonyl carbon, so the branch is at C3, not C2.
Only one group on nitrogen is ethyl; the other is methyl.
The N-ethyl group is not part of the parent chain; the parent is only the acyl chain, which has four carbons.

q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
h: When a –COX group is attached to a ring, the carbonyl carbon is not part of the ring. Which suffix handles that case?
w: The C(=O)Cl carbon is outside the ring, so the ring name takes the suffix -carbonyl (as in cyclohexanecarboxylic acid → cyclohexanecarbonyl chloride). The answer is cyclohexanecarbonyl chloride.
x: The carbonyl carbon is not one of the ring atoms, so the compound is not a seven-carbon ring acyl chloride.
A chloroformate is Cl–C(=O)–O–R, with an oxygen between the ring and the carbonyl; here the ring carbon is bonded directly to C=O.
This is a ring ketone with Cl on a ring carbon; the compound shown has Cl on the carbonyl carbon outside the ring.

q: What is the name of the compound shown?
h: Look at what links the two C=O groups. Then name each acyl half as its acid.
w: Two acyl groups joined through one oxygen make an anhydride. One half is acetyl (2 C), the other propanoyl (3 C). A mixed anhydride lists both acids alphabetically: acetic propanoic anhydride.
x: Propanoic anhydride has two propanoyl groups (six carbons); this compound has five carbons, with one acetyl half.
Acetic anhydride has two acetyl groups (four carbons); one half here is propanoyl.
Propyl acetate is an ester (one C=O); the compound shown has two C=O groups joined by an oxygen.

q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>C≡N?
h: In the -nitrile suffix the C≡N carbon is counted as C1 of the chain.
w: The chain is N≡C(1)–CH2(2)–CH(3)(CH3)–CH3(4): four carbons including the nitrile carbon, so butanenitrile, methyl at C3: 3-methylbutanenitrile.
x: This leaves out the nitrile carbon. With the -nitrile suffix the C≡N carbon is C1, so the chain has four carbons.
Numbering starts at the nitrile carbon, which puts the branch at C3, not C2.
There are only four carbons in the longest chain that contains the C≡N carbon (five carbons in total, one being the methyl branch).

h: Lactam = cyclic amide; the Greek letter names the carbon bonded to nitrogen (α is next to C=O).
w: In a lactam the ring N is bonded to the C=O. Greek letters count from the carbon next to C=O: α, β, γ, δ. A δ-lactam has N on the δ-carbon, so the ring holds C=O + 4 carbons + N = a six-membered ring: A, piperidin-2-one.
x: This is a five-membered cyclic amide (N on the γ-carbon): a γ-lactam.
C has a ring oxygen, not nitrogen: it is a δ-lactone (cyclic ester).
This is a four-membered cyclic amide, the β-lactam ring of penicillins.

q: Which carboxylic acid is the strongest acid?
h: An electronegative atom stabilizes the carboxylate by induction, and that effect fades quickly with distance.
w: The C–Cl dipole pulls electron density from the carboxylate and stabilizes it. Induction weakens sharply with each intervening σ bond, so the Cl on the α-carbon has the biggest effect: A, 2-chlorobutanoic acid (pKa ≈ 2.9) vs 3-chloro (≈ 4.1), 4-chloro (≈ 4.5) and butanoic acid (≈ 4.8).
x: Cl on the β-carbon still helps, but one more bond away from the carboxylate it has a much smaller effect than α-Cl.
Cl on the γ-carbon is so far away that the pK<sub>a</sub> is only slightly lower than butanoic acid.
Butanoic acid has no electron-withdrawing group and is the weakest of the four.

q: Rank the three acids in order of increasing acidity (weakest first).
h: Compare the inductive pull of one F with one Cl first, then ask what a second Cl adds.
w: All three are stabilized by induction at the α-carbon. F is more electronegative than Cl, so FCH2COOH (pKa 2.6) is stronger than ClCH2COOH (2.9). Two Cl atoms add their effects, so Cl2CHCOOH (1.3) is much stronger than either monohalo acid. Order: I < III < II.
x: This makes Cl more withdrawing than F; fluorine is the more electronegative atom, so fluoroacetic acid is the stronger of the two monohalo acids.
This puts fluoroacetic acid above dichloroacetic acid. Two α-chlorines together outweigh one fluorine.
This reverses the effect of halogens: more and stronger electron-withdrawing groups make the acid stronger, not weaker.

q: Which benzoic acid has the highest pKa?
h: A para substituent that donates electrons by resonance destabilizes the carboxylate anion.
w: Electron-withdrawing groups stabilize the benzoate anion (lower pKa); electron donors destabilize it (higher pKa). Para-OCH3 donates by resonance more than it withdraws by induction, so A, 4-methoxybenzoic acid is the weakest acid (pKa ≈ 4.5) vs benzoic acid (4.2), 4-chlorobenzoic acid (4.0) and 4-nitrobenzoic acid (3.4).
x: Benzoic acid is the reference (4.2); a para-methoxy group makes the acid weaker still.
Cl withdraws inductively more than it donates, so 4-chlorobenzoic acid is a slightly stronger acid than benzoic acid.
NO<sub>2</sub> withdraws strongly by induction and resonance, so 4-nitrobenzoic acid is the strongest acid of the four (lowest pK<sub>a</sub>).

q: A mixture of benzoic acid (pK<sub>a</sub> 4.2) and phenol (pK<sub>a</sub> 10.0) is dissolved in diethyl ether. Which aqueous solution extracts the benzoic acid but leaves the phenol in the ether layer? (H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> pK<sub>a</sub> 6.4, H<sub>2</sub>O 15.7, CH<sub>3</sub>OH 15.5)
h: A base deprotonates an acid substantially only when the conjugate acid of the base is weaker (higher pK<sub>a</sub>) than the acid.
w: Bicarbonate's conjugate acid is H2CO3 (pKa 6.4). Benzoic acid (4.2) is stronger, so it is converted to water-soluble sodium benzoate; phenol (10.0) is weaker than H2CO3, so it stays neutral in the ether. The answer is NaHCO3.
x: Hydroxide (conjugate acid pK<sub>a</sub> 15.7) deprotonates both acids, so both would move into the water.
Methoxide (conjugate acid pK<sub>a</sub> 15.5) is also strong enough to deprotonate phenol, so it does not separate the two.
Acid keeps both compounds neutral, so neither moves into the aqueous layer.

q: Rank the compounds in order of decreasing reactivity toward nucleophilic acyl substitution (most reactive first).
h: Two factors: how much the group on the acyl carbon donates by resonance, and how good it is as a leaving group.
w: II (acid chloride): Cl donates very little into the C=O and Cl− is an excellent leaving group. IV (anhydride): the bridging O is shared by two C=O groups, so it donates less to each, and a carboxylate leaves well. I (ester): OR donates more and RO− is a poorer leaving group. III (amide): N is the best π donor and R2N− is the worst leaving group. Order: II > IV > I > III.
x: An anhydride is less reactive than an acid chloride: its carboxylate leaving group is poorer than chloride, and its oxygen donates more into the C=O than Cl does.
This makes the amide more reactive than the ester. Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so it donates its lone pair more strongly, and amide ions are terrible leaving groups.
This puts the ester above the anhydride. The anhydride's bridging oxygen is split between two carbonyls and its leaving group is a resonance-stabilized carboxylate, so it is more reactive.

q:
Which statements help explain why amides are the least reactive carboxylic acid derivatives toward nucleophiles?
I. The nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the C=O, making the carbonyl carbon less electrophilic.
II. The amide C–N bond has partial double-bond character.
III. An amide ion (R2N−) is a very poor leaving group.
IV. Amides cannot form a tetrahedral intermediate because nitrogen has no lone pair.
h: Draw the resonance form of an amide that has C=N. Then ask how basic each possible leaving group is.
w: The N lone pair donates strongly into the C=O (I), which is exactly why the C–N bond has partial double-bond character (II, planar amide, restricted rotation). The leaving group would be R2N−, conjugate base of an amine (pKa ≈ 35), so it leaves very poorly (III). Statement IV is false: amide nitrogen does have a lone pair (that is the source of I), and amides do react through tetrahedral intermediates under forcing conditions. Answer: I, II and III only.
x: Statement II is true and is a direct consequence of I: the resonance donation shows up as C–N double-bond character.
Statement IV is false: amide nitrogen has a lone pair, and amides are hydrolyzed through tetrahedral intermediates on heating with acid or base.
Statement IV is false, so the set with all four cannot be right.

q: Which reaction proceeds in good yield simply by mixing the two reagents (with a weak base such as pyridine where HCl forms)?
h: Nucleophilic acyl substitution runs downhill: from a more reactive derivative to a less reactive one.
w: Acyl substitutions go from a higher rung of the reactivity ladder to a lower one, because the nucleophile must be a poorer leaving group than the group it replaces. Acid chloride → ester is downhill (Cl− leaves, the alcohol stays): CH3COCl + ethanol → ethyl acetate.
x: Ester → acid chloride is uphill: chloride is a much better leaving group than methoxide, so Cl<sup>−</sup> cannot push out CH<sub>3</sub>O<sup>−</sup>.
Amide → ester is uphill: a neutral alcohol cannot displace NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>, a far worse leaving group than an alkoxide.
A carboxylate is the least reactive acyl species of all (its negative charge repels nucleophiles), so methanol cannot add to it.

q: Acetyl chloride reacts with methylamine. Which species is the first-formed tetrahedral intermediate?
h: The amine nitrogen attacks the carbonyl carbon; the π electrons go onto oxygen. Nothing has left yet.
w: Addition of the neutral amine to the C=O gives a tetrahedral carbon bearing O<sup>−</sup>, Cl and a positively charged N (it has given its lone pair to carbon). Next the C=O re-forms and expels Cl<sup>−</sup>, then a base removes the N–H proton to give the amide.
x: This is formed after the tetrahedral intermediate collapses and chloride leaves; its carbon is trigonal, not tetrahedral.
This is the neutral amide product, after loss of both Cl<sup>−</sup> and a proton.
An acylium ion is not on this pathway; an amine attacks the neutral acid chloride directly by addition–elimination.

q: The energy diagram shows the hydrolysis of methyl acetate by hydroxide. What does point B represent?
c: the transition state for addition of hydroxide
the acylium ion formed when methoxide leaves
the carboxylate ion formed by proton transfer
h: Points at maxima are transition states; local minima between maxima are intermediates.
w: Nucleophilic acyl substitution is addition–elimination. A is the TS for hydroxide adding to C=O, B is the minimum between the two barriers: the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate. C is the TS for loss of methoxide. The final deep drop is the fast proton transfer that gives acetate.
x: A transition state sits at an energy maximum; B is a local minimum.
No acylium ion forms in base; the C=O re-forms as methoxide is expelled from the tetrahedral intermediate.
The carboxylate forms at the end of the reaction (the products), after the second barrier, not between the two barriers.
